Gas Day: explainer storyboard

2:40 in 7 scenes. Every frame here is a real frame of the application, captured by python film/render.py --storyboard. The narration, camera moves and on-screen labels come from film/scenes.js. Filmed on flow data to 2026-06-30.

0:00Beneath your feet

Shows
The flow map on its own, full screen, on the latest gas day.
Camera
Fades up from black high over Canada, then pushes in and tilts along the network.
Sound
A low pad fades in under the first line.

0:01Right now, natural gas is moving beneath your feet. Across mountains, prairie and shield, through steel you will never see.

0:09This is twenty years of that movement, drawn from public records, on a single map.

0:16How to read the map

Shows
The whole application: map, legend, time bar and chart panel. Line width, colour and pulses.
Camera
Levels out as the app slides in around the map, then flies west into Alberta.
Sound
The pad opens up. A soft pulse starts.

0:18This is Gas Day. Every line follows a route on TC Energy's Canadian network, and every number comes from flow data filed with the Canada Energy Regulator.

0:29Thick lines carry more gas. Brighter blue means a route is closer to full. And the pulses show which way the gas is flowing.

0:38Twenty years in twenty seconds

Shows
The time slider playing from 2006 to the latest gas day, with the throughput chart following.
Camera
Pulls back to the whole network and holds while the years run.
Sound
The pulse quickens and the pad lifts through the time-lapse.

0:39Press play, and twenty years run past in seconds. More than seven thousand days of flow.

0:45Watch the west. In 2010, about five billion cubic feet a day came down this corridor, out of Alberta and British Columbia.

0:54By 2025, it was more than twelve.

0:58The pipe that changed direction

Shows
Clicking a key point. The pulses at Niagara reverse between 2007 and 2025. The net exports chart.
Camera
Dives from the whole network to the Niagara River, then lifts over southern Ontario.
Sound
The pulse drops out for the reveal, then returns.

1:00Click any point, and the panel tells its story. This is Niagara, on the border with New York.

1:06In 2007, gas flowed east here, out of Canada, at around eight hundred million cubic feet a day.

1:13Then American shale changed everything. Watch the pulses. By 2025, the same pipe was carrying gas the other way, into Ontario.

1:23One chart shows the whole border shifting, region by region.

1:28The coldest week

Shows
January 2024 at the Calgary key point: the headline numbers, the weather scatter and the utilization grid.
Camera
Crosses the continent to Calgary and settles low over the city.
Sound
The pad darkens and thins. A cold, high tone.

1:30January 2024. An Arctic front settles over the prairies, and Calgary's average temperature falls to minus thirty-four.

1:39Gas delivered toward the city jumps by more than half in a week, to the highest level this point has ever recorded.

1:46Here, every dot is one day. The colder it gets, the further right it sits, and the more gas this point moves.

1:53And one grid shows, month by month, which points are running close to full.

1:58Fire season

Shows
The wildfire layer: burned areas for the slider year, live satellite hotspots, and the burned-area chart.
Camera
Rises north over the boreal forest, tilted, and drifts east across the 2023 burn scars.
Sound
A low swell as the burned areas appear.

2:00Now switch on the wildfire layer, and go back to the summer of 2023. The worst fire season Canada has ever recorded.

2:09Each orange shape is a large fire. By this map's estimate, more than half a million hectares burned within fifty kilometres of these routes that year.

2:19And the red dots are live: satellite hotspots from the last twenty-four hours.

2:24Only public data

Shows
The map alone again on the latest gas day, then the end card with the data sources.
Camera
The app slides away and the camera pulls back to the whole network.
Sound
The pad resolves and fades.

2:26No private feeds. No licences. Only public data, a time slider, and a new way to see a network that never stops.

2:35This is Gas Day.
